title: How did farming change human societies?
essentialQuestion: What changed when some communities began producing food?
learningGoal: Explain how farming led to surplus food, new kinds of work and trade, and describe one problem it brought.

warmUp.question: Is it easier to find food in the wild or to grow it? Why?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which way of life seems safer to you? What else would you want to know before you decide?

cards.title: Two ways of life in Harapan Valley
rows: Wild fruit, roots, fish and animals, found in different places each season
Grain they plant and goats they keep
They move to different places during the year
They stay in mud-brick houses all year
A lot, after a good harvest

sections.heading: Farming began in many places
sections.text: For most of human history, people got their food by foraging. They gathered wild plants, hunted animals and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to plant seeds and keep animals. Farming did not start in just one place or at one time, and different parts of the world grew different crops. Farmers in West Asia grew wheat and barley, while farmers in China grew rice and millet. People in New Guinea grew bananas and taro, and people in Mexico grew maize and beans. People in the Andes mountains first farmed potatoes, and people in parts of Africa first farmed sorghum. In Harapan Valley, one group still moves around to find food, while the other group farms.
sections.simpler: Long ago, people got food by foraging. They picked wild plants and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to farm. They planted seeds and kept animals. Farming began in many places at different times. Each place had its own crops. West Asia grew wheat, and China grew rice. Mexico grew corn. Parts of Africa grew other grains. In Harapan Valley, one group moves to find food. The other group farms.

sections.heading: Extra food changed work and trade
sections.text: Farming could grow a lot of food in a small area. After a good harvest, a village might have a surplus, which is more food than people need right away. With extra grain in store, not everyone had to farm, so some people could specialise in making pots, cloth or tools. In Harapan Valley, one family makes clay pots and gives them to farmers in exchange for grain. This is a kind of trade. Villages also traded with each other, and a village near the sea might trade salt for grain. Over time, some farming villages grew into towns.
sections.simpler: A farm can grow lots of food in a small space. After a good year, there may be a surplus of extra food. People keep it safe for later. Now not everyone has to farm, so some people can specialise. They do one main job, like making pots. In Harapan Valley, one family makes pots. They give pots and get grain. This is trade. Villages trade with each other too, and some grow into towns.

sections.heading: Farming also brought new problems
sections.text: Farming was hard work, with long days of planting, watering and harvesting. Many villages depended on only a few crops. If the rain did not come, the harvest could fail and people had little to eat. Living close to animals and to many other people also helped some illnesses spread. In some places, a few families took control of more land and stored grain, which gave them more power. Not every group chose to farm, and many kept foraging or did some of both. So historians ask a careful question: was farming better, and better for whom?
sections.simpler: Farming is hard work. Many villages grow only a few crops. If no rain comes, the crops can die. Then there is not much to eat. People live close to animals and to each other, so sickness can spread. Some families get more land and food. This gives them more power. Not every group chooses to farm. Many keep foraging. So we ask: was farming better? Who was it better for?

glossary.definition: Finding wild food, like fruit, roots, fish and animals, instead of growing it.
glossary.example: The group in Harapan Valley lives by foraging for fruit, roots and fish.

glossary.definition: A plant that people grow for food or to use.
glossary.example: Rice was an important crop in early China.

glossary.definition: More food or goods than people need right now.
glossary.example: After a good harvest, the farming village keeps its surplus grain in a store.

glossary.definition: To do mostly one kind of work and get good at it.
glossary.example: In Harapan Valley, one family specialises in making clay pots.

glossary.definition: Giving something to someone and getting something else back.
glossary.example: The potter family trades clay pots for grain.

options.text: In many places, at different times
options.feedback: Yes. Farming started in West Asia, China, Mexico, Africa and more. Each place had its own crops.

options.text: In one village, on one special day
options.feedback: Not quite. Farming did not start in just one place. Look again at the first part of the reading.

options.text: Only in places close to the sea
options.feedback: Not quite. The reading names places far from the sea too, like the Andes mountains. Look again at the first part.

checks.question: How could a surplus let some people specialise?

options.text: It made farming work very quick and easy
options.feedback: Not quite. Farming was still hard work. Look at what stored food made possible in the second part.

options.text: It gave every family the same amount of food
options.feedback: Not quite. The reading says some families got more than others. Look at the second part about stored food.

options.text: Stored food meant fewer people had to farm
options.feedback: Yes. With extra food in store, some people could make pots, cloth or tools instead of farming.

checks.question: Was farming better for everyone? Think of both groups in the valley.

write.prompt: Was early farming good for everyone? Give one way it helped people and one problem it brought. Use evidence from the lesson.
sentenceStarters: One example from the lesson is ...
But farming also brought a problem: ...
selfCheck: I gave one way farming helped people.
I gave one problem farming brought.
I used an example from the lesson.
write.example: Farming helped people because it could grow a lot of food in one place. One example from the lesson is the farming village in Harapan Valley. After a good harvest, it has a surplus of grain. This lets one family specialise in making pots. But farming also brought a problem: the village grows only a few crops. If the rain does not come, the whole harvest can fail. This was hard for families with no extra land or grain. So I think farming was important, but it was not better for everyone.

speak.independentTask: Explain out loud how a surplus can lead to trade. Try: First ... Then ... So ...

watch.title: The Neolithic Revolution: Why Was Agriculture So Important?
watch.why: This short video explains how farming changed where people lived, the work they did and who had power.
watch.beforeQuestion: Watch for one good change and one problem that farming brought.
watch.afterQuestion: Does the video say farming was good for everyone? Give one detail.
watch.summary: This video explains why farming was such a big change in human history. For a very long time, people found their food in the wild. Then people in several parts of the world began to grow crops and keep animals. Farming could make more food in a smaller area. So more people could live in one place, and villages could grow. Stored food let some people do other work, like making tools or trading. Some people became leaders. Farming also changed the land around people. But farming brought risks too. A bad harvest could mean hunger. Illness could spread more easily. Some people got much more land and power than others. Farming was very important, but it did not make life better for everyone in the same way.
keyPoints: Farming began in several parts of the world, not just one.
Extra food let villages grow and let people do new kinds of work.
Farming brought risks too, and its good things were not shared equally.

visual.description: A simple world map with small crop pictures in six regions where people began farming on their own: wheat and barley with goats (West Asia), rice and millet (China), bananas and taro (New Guinea), maize, beans and squash (Mexico and Central America), potatoes (the Andes in South America), and sorghum and millet (parts of Africa south of the Sahara). No arrows join the regions, because each began farming separately. Caption: 'Farming began in many places, at different times.'
visual.alt: World map with crop pictures in six regions where farming began separately, such as wheat in West Asia, rice in China, bananas in New Guinea and maize in Mexico.

sensitiveNotes: Section 3 mentions failed harvests and hunger. Some learners may have lived through food shortages, so keep the discussion general and let them use the fictional village rather than their own experience.
educatorNotes: Harapan Valley is fictional. You could swap its grain and goats for crops and animals your learners know, such as cassava, rice or chickens.
Dates are rounded on purpose ('more than 10,000 years ago'). Farming began at different times in different regions; avoid presenting one region as first or best, or foragers as 'behind'.
changes: Rewrote the reading at about grade 5–6 (Base44 was about grade 10–11) and cut it from four sections to three.
Wrote a new simpler English version from scratch in short sentences; Base44's version was almost a copy of the original.
Added named crops from West Asia, China, New Guinea, Mexico, the Andes and Africa, so farming is shown beginning in many places.
Turned the two Harapan Valley lists into one comparison table and used the valley in all three reading sections and the example answer.

New glossary (foraging, crop, surplus, specialise, trade); every word now appears in both the text and the simpler text. Dropped 'domestication' and 'inequality' and explained the ideas in plain words instead.
Added a warm-up, a visual plan and a three-item self-check; rewrote the checks so the correct answers sit in different positions.
Rewrote the video questions, summary and key points at a lower reading level; added a UNESCO source for New Guinea.
